name: Variable resistance training (bands and chains)

lead: Variable resistance training attaches bands or chains to a barbell so the weight gets heavier as the lift progresses, matching the way people are stronger at the top of a squat or press than at the bottom. Lifters use it to train strength and explosive power, which supports building a more muscular body.

Meta-analyses of studies comparing it with conventional training report greater strength gains in some analyses and no significant difference in others, and acute studies report higher bar velocity and power.

paras: Lifters loop elastic bands or hang chains from the bar on exercises such as the bench press and squat, alongside normal programs. The added tension is small at the bottom of the lift and larger near lockout.

Risks resemble those of heavy barbell training in general, such as strain from poor setup or equipment failure. Bands and chains add setup complexity, and a band snapping or a bar loading unevenly is a practical hazard.

angle.text: VRT is a way of loading lifts differently. Lifters use it to train strength and explosive power as part of programs aimed at building a muscular physique.

lead: Variable resistance training (VRT), also called accommodating resistance, changes the load across a lift by adding elastic bands or chains to a barbell. As the bar rises, bands stretch or more chain links leave the floor, so the resistance increases where a lifter is mechanically strongest [1][2].

The appearance payoff is through training outcomes: more strength and power, which lifters use to progress the lifts and the physique work that builds a more muscular, athletic look. Muscular strength is treated in sports science as a foundation for performance and health [1]. Bands and chains became widely known through the Westside Barbell gym of powerlifter Louie Simmons and his conjugate method, in which they modify squat, bench press and deadlift variations [3][4].

Research shows mixed results. A 2022 meta-analysis of 14 studies reported that VRT produced larger maximal-strength gains than constant-resistance training, with an effect size of 0.80 [2]. A separate 2022 meta-analysis of 17 studies in healthy adults reported no statistically significant difference in maximal strength between the approaches [5]. An earlier 2015 meta-analysis found a 5 kg mean advantage in the one-repetition maximum but is listed as retracted [6]. A 2022 analysis of acute studies reported higher bar velocity and power with VRT [7], and a 2026 meta-analysis in athletes reported improvements in jumping, sprinting and change-of-direction performance [8].

Higher mean velocity and power in a 2022 meta-analysis of 16 crossover studies [7]

paras: In a normal barbell lift the weight is constant while the lifter's leverage changes, so the bottom of a lift is often harder than the top. Bands and chains make the resistance rise through the lift to match leverage. Reviews describe the aim as improved rate of force development, coordination between muscles, motor-unit recruitment and a smaller drop in force at the sticking point [6].

Resistance bands were originally made from surgical tubing and used in rehabilitation, and later spread to general fitness and strength training; they are usually colour-coded by resistance level, with the codes varying by brand [9]. In VRT, loop bands are anchored to the floor or a rack and attached to the bar so tension rises as the bar goes up, being smallest at the bottom of the lift and greatest near lockout. A 2016 study examined elastic bands as a component of periodised resistance training [10].
Chains are hung from the bar so that links lift off the floor as the lifter rises, adding load progressively. Gyms with racks, monolifts and specialty bars commonly stock them alongside bands [11].

Louie Simmons (1947 to 2022), an American powerlifter and coach who entered his first meet in 1966, founded the invitation-only Westside Barbell gym in Columbus, Ohio, and developed the conjugate method, adapted from Soviet and Bulgarian training protocols and known for using bands and chains on strength exercises [3]. The method rotates special exercises at least every three weeks and alternates max-effort sessions with dynamic-effort sessions of submaximal weight lifted at maximal speed [3][4]. Simmons also publicly defended performance-enhancing drugs and said he had used anabolic steroids since 1970 [3][4].

Earlier academic comparisons of variable and constant resistance existed: a randomised trial of variable versus constant resistance strength training in adult males was published in 1978 [12]. Recent studies have also taken velocity-based approaches to training with bands [13][14].

sections.h: Use in strength and physique training
paras: Westside-influenced training is discussed on T Nation, where one member notes that when people mention conjugate training for raw lifting, many think only of bands, chains, boards and box squats while overlooking other elements, and others confess to never having implemented band and chain work [15][16]. A member describing a local gym lists bands, chains, boxes and specialty bars among its equipment [11].

In practical terms lifters use VRT to place more load near lockout on lifts such as the bench press and squat, alongside normal programmes, to train bar speed and strength through the full range [2][7].

On acute performance, a 2022 meta-analysis of 16 crossover studies with 207 participants reported that VRT produced greater mean velocity (standardized mean difference 0.675) and mean power (1.022) than constant resistance [7]. Long-term results differ between analyses. One 2022 meta-analysis of 14 studies favoured VRT for maximal strength in all subjects and in trained subjects (effect size 0.57), and found a significantly larger gain in trained subjects with loads of at least 80 percent of one-repetition maximum, while another that included 17 studies and 491 healthy adults (341 men and 150 women, aged 18 to 37) reported no statistically significant difference in maximal strength for lower or upper body [2][5].

A 2026 meta-analysis of 15 articles with 442 athletes reported that VRT improved jumping, sprint and change-of-direction performance [8]. Other trials have used VRT in older women with elastic bands over 32 weeks, in surgically menopausal women alongside estrogen therapy, and in paediatric cancer survivors, outcomes outside the physique context [17][18][19].

Risks resemble those of heavy barbell training in general, and the practical hazards include setup complexity, equipment failure and uneven loading. Perceived-effort studies of elastic band training have examined psychological and physical predictors of effort [14].

Meta-analyses of controlled training studies have compared VRT with constant-resistance training for maximal strength, power and velocity in healthy adults; their findings are summarised under Effectiveness [2][7][5]. A 1978 randomised trial compared variable and constant resistance in adult males [12], and a velocity-based study examined repetitions to failure with bands in the bench press [13]. Muscle-size outcomes were not the main focus of the meta-analyses described here.

lore.intro: On T Nation, bands and chains are discussed mainly through Westside and conjugate training, with members trading logs and noting that the practice is often reduced to its equipment [15][16].
